title: The Transnational Responsibility of the Mexican Vote in the United States
author: María Elena Valdivia
content:
_This article by María Elena Valdivia appears in the November 2026 issue of_
Let's Talk About Migration _(_ Hablemos de Migración _), a magazine on
migration issues published by the Frente Amplio de Mexicanos y Migrantes.[Read
and download the full November
issue](https://diegotorres72.com/internacional/boletin-hablemos-de-
migracion-2/)._

![Let's Talk About Migration](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2025/06/image-1.png)

“Citizenship doesn’t end at the border; neither does responsibility.” This
statement summarizes a reality that defines the Mexican population living in
the United States today: more than 38 million people of Mexican origin,
according to the US Census Bureau, American Community Survey (ACS) 2025, they
reside in a country whose institutional decisions directly affect Mexicans in
transit, in detention, and returning. This presence is not merely demographic;
it is political. In this context, the electoral participation of citizens of
Mexican descent—whether by naturalization or birth—takes on a dimension that
transcends the domestic sphere of the United States: it becomes a form of
transnational responsibility.

The Mexican community in the United States is one of the largest transnational
populations in the world. Its political influence has grown steadily: the Pew
Research Center reports that, between 2020 and 2025, the number of registered
voters of Mexican origin increased, especially among young binational
citizens. This increase is not merely statistical; it is structural. It
implies that a growing number of people are participating in a political
system whose decisions have direct effects on Mexican communities on the move.
Citizenship in the United States does not sever ties with Mexico; rather, it
transforms them into a responsibility that operates in two directions: toward
the country of residence and toward the Mexican communities affected by U.S.
immigration policies.

Between January 2025 and October 2026, the Government the Government
Accountability Office (GAO) released audits documenting persistent failures at
ICE detention centers: deficiencies in medical oversight, delays in emergency
care, non-compliance with minimum standards, inconsistent surveillance
practices, and failures in crisis response protocols. In previous audits, the
GAO has highlighted cases where a lack of timely medical attention led to
serious hospitalizations, and where the absence of clear protocols increased
risks for people in custody. These failures are not abstract; they affect real
lives. And they show that the protection of people in custody remains an
institutional problem that is rarely corrected without public pressure. This
evidence is central to understanding why voter participation in the United
States is politically relevant: the vote influences the system that defines
immigration policies and detention practices that directly impact Mexicans
beyond the border.

![The Transnational Responsibility of the Mexican Vote in the United
States](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/ltam-
nov26-08-body-p34.jpg)Illustration: _Let 's Talk About Migration_, November
2026

Voting is not an isolated act. It is a form of binational influence. Every
vote cast by a citizen of Mexican origin impacts decisions that determine
detention standards, oversight resources, domestic operations, racial
profiling practices, and budgetary priorities related to immigration. In other
words, participating in elections in the United States is exercising a form of
transnational responsibility, because it connects daily life in the country of
residence with institutional decisions that impact Mexican communities on the
move. Voting not only expresses political preferences; it protects lives. It
not only participates in American democracy; it influences the Mexican migrant
experience.

This electoral responsibility is amplified when it is articulated with civic
practices that sustain and expand its political impact. In the United States,
pro - migrant civil society organizations with a Mexican and Latin American
presence have played an important role in documenting the effects of
immigration policies, providing basic guidance during administrative
processes, bringing public visibility to cases that often fall outside
institutional scrutiny, preparing reports for local and federal authorities,
participating in public hearings on surveillance practices, and disseminating
information about rights during immigration operations. These actions do not
replace the State, but they do contribute to addressing shortcomings
documented by the GAO and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) issues
should be known and discussed in public and legislative spaces.

The transition between these two spheres—the electoral and the civic—is
fundamental: community action produces evidence and visibility; electoral
participation transforms that evidence into institutional influence. Civil
society organizations generate information that allows voters to make informed
decisions about migration policies, while the vote influences the
institutional framework that regulates the practices these organizations
monitor. This interaction creates a binational political circuit: the
community documents, makes visible, and provides support; voting citizens
transform that information into decisions that affect real lives.

Voting in the United States is not an isolated, individual act. It is
participating from a position of citizenship that coexists with a profoundly
unequal reality: millions of Mexicans who are part of our daily lives—family,
friends, coworkers, community members—do not have access to immigration
regularization or the right to vote, even though they live, work, and
contribute to the same country. This inequality is not abstract. It is a daily
experience. It is the political distance between those who can decide and
those who, despite sharing a home, history, and community, are excluded from
the democratic process that defines their destiny.

![The Transnational Responsibility of the Mexican Vote in the United
States](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/ltam-
nov26-08-body-p35.jpg)Illustration: _Let 's Talk About Migration_, November
2026

In this context, the electoral participation of citizens of Mexican origin
takes on an ethical and political dimension that transcends the individual
sphere. It is a transnational responsibility that protects real lives, because
the decisions made at the ballot box determine whether the people we love will
be recognized as subjects of rights or reduced, once again, to the obsessively
repeated category of “illegals” by political actors who solicit our vote while
denigrating those who are part of our lives. Exercising citizenship in the
United States, then, is an act of accepting or rejecting this contradiction.
It implies recognizing that the vote not only expresses political preferences
but also defines the conditions of existence of those who share our history,
our language, and our mobility.

The question for the Mexican diaspora—naturalized, binational, and Mexican-
American—is unavoidable and profoundly political: what does it mean to
exercise citizenship in a country where millions of people we love are
violated, made invisible, or criminalized by those who seek our vote?

Responding to it—at the ballot box and in everyday civic life—is not a
symbolic gesture. It is fully assuming the transnational responsibility of
living, working, and loving in a country where immigration policy defines the
destiny of our communities, and acting accordingly.
